key_terms.meaning: A function of an independent variable that carries information, written x(t) in continuous time or x[n] in discrete time.
A signal defined for every real value of time t, such as x(t)=sin(2πft).
A signal defined only at integer index n, such as x[n]=0.8ⁿ for n≥0.
The value x[n]=x(nTₛ) of a continuous-time signal taken at t=nTₛ, where Tₛ is the sampling interval.
An operator that maps an input signal x to an output signal y, written y=T{x}.
An energy signal has finite E=∫|x(t)|²dt; a power signal has finite nonzero average P=lim_{T→∞}(1/2T)∫_{-T}^{T}|x(t)|²dt.
A signal that repeats after a period T>0, so x(t+T)=x(t) for all t; the smallest such T is the fundamental period.
x(t) is even if x(−t)=x(t), odd if x(−t)=−x(t); every signal splits into even plus odd parts.
δ(t) is a generalized pulse with unit area, δ(t)=0 for t≠0 and ∫δ(t)dt=1; in discrete time δ[n]=1 at n=0 and 0 elsewhere.
u(t)=0 for t<0 and u(t)=1 for t>0; in discrete time u[n]=1 for n≥0 and 0 for n<0.
r(t)=t u(t), zero for t<0 and rising linearly for t≥0; in discrete time r[n]=n u[n].
x(t)=A·exp(st), where A is amplitude and s=σ+jω is complex; real s gives growth or decay, imaginary s gives sinusoids.
Replacing x(t) by x(t−t₀) moves the signal right by t₀ when t₀>0.
Replacing x(t) by x(at) compresses the signal in time when |a|>1 and stretches it when 0<|a|<1.
Replacing x(t) by x(−t) flips the signal about t=0.
A system is linear if it obeys superposition: T{a x₁+b x₂}=a T{x₁}+b T{x₂} for all inputs and constants.
A system is time-invariant if a delayed input gives the same output delayed by the same amount: x(t−t₀)→y(t−t₀).
A system is causal if its output at any time depends only on present and past inputs, not future inputs.
A system is bounded-input bounded-output stable if every bounded input produces a bounded output.
Two signals are orthogonal on an interval if their inner product is zero, ∫x(t)y*(t)dt=0; such signals can form a basis.

takeaways: A signal is a function of an independent variable that carries information, and a system maps input signals to output signals.
Continuous-time signals use real t and discrete-time signals use integer n; a sample is x[n]=x(nTₛ).
Energy and power classify signals by finite energy or finite nonzero average power, while periodic, even, and odd properties simplify later work.
The impulse, step, ramp, and exponential are standard building blocks and common test inputs for systems.
Operations on the independent variable change the graph: shifting moves it, scaling compresses or stretches it, and reversal flips it.
A system is CT or DT by the variable of its input and output, and its properties must be tested from definitions.
Linearity, time invariance, causality, and BIBO stability are separate tests; one does not automatically imply another.
Signals on an interval behave like vectors: inner products measure similarity and orthogonal sets form a basis.
Parseval's relation gives signal energy from the coefficients of an orthogonal expansion.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for precise definitions, correct sketches, property tests, and short derivations that connect impulse, step, ramp, signal operations, and system properties.

bank.q: Define a signal and a system. Distinguish continuous-time and discrete-time signals with one example and one sketch description for each.
outline: Signal definition: function of an independent variable carrying information
System definition: operator mapping input to output
CT uses real t, DT uses integer n
Examples: x(t)=sin(2πft), x[n]=0.8ⁿu[n]
Sketch: continuous curve versus stem plot

bank.q: Classify a signal by energy, power, periodicity, and even or odd symmetry. Give the defining equation and one test for each class.
outline: Energy definition E=∫|x(t)|²dt and finite-energy test
Power definition P=lim average of |x(t)|² and finite nonzero test
Periodic test x(t+T)=x(t); fundamental period is smallest T
Even test x(−t)=x(t), odd test x(−t)=−x(t)
Even and odd decomposition formula

bank.q: Define the unit impulse, unit step, ramp, and exponential signals. State the relations among impulse, step, and ramp in continuous time.
outline: Impulse: zero except at origin, unit area
Step: zero before origin, one after origin
Ramp: t u(t)
Exponential: A·exp(st), with real or complex s
Relations: step is integral of impulse, ramp is integral of step, impulse is generalized derivative of step

bank.q: Explain time shifting, time scaling, and time reversal on x(t). For y(t)=x(2t−6), state the correct order of operations.
outline: x(t−t₀) shifts right for t₀>0
x(at) compresses for |a|>1 and stretches for 0<|a|<1
x(−t) reverses about t=0
x(2t−6)=x(2(t−3)): scale by 2 then shift right by 3
Equivalent order: shift right by 6 then scale by 2

bank.q: Define a continuous-time system and a discrete-time system. Give one electrical example of each and identify input and output.
outline: CT system: input x(t) gives output y(t) for real t
DT system: input x[n] gives output y[n] for integer n
Electrical CT example: RC low-pass filter with voltage input and output
Electrical DT example: digital filter acting on sampled sequence
State input and output variables clearly

bank.q: Given x(t)=u(t+1)−u(t−2), sketch x(t), find its even and odd parts, and state whether it is an energy or power signal.
outline: Pulse of height 1 from t=−1 to t=2
Even part xₑ(t)=[x(t)+x(−t)]/2
Odd part x₀(t)=[x(t)−x(−t)]/2
Energy E=∫|x(t)|²dt=3
Finite energy means energy signal; average power is zero

bank.q: Using unit step functions, write a rectangular pulse p(t) of height A and width W centred at t=0. Sketch p(2t+4) and p(−t+1).
outline: p(2t+4)=p(2(t+2)): centre at t=−2 and width W/2
p(−t+1)=p(−(t−1)): centre at t=1 and width W
Correct amplitude A in both sketches
Step functions mark the pulse edges

bank.q: Test the system y(t)=t x(t) for linearity, time invariance, causality, and BIBO stability. Show the steps.
outline: Linearity: T{a x₁+b x₂}=t(a x₁+b x₂)=a y₁+b y₂
Time invariance: input x(t−t₀) gives t x(t−t₀), not (t−t₀)x(t−t₀)
Causality: output at t uses input at same t only
Stability: bounded |x|≤M gives |y|≤M|t|, which is unbounded as |t|→∞
Conclusion: linear, time-varying, causal, not BIBO stable

bank.q: Test the discrete-time system y[n]=x[n]+x[n−1] for linearity, time invariance, causality, and BIBO stability. Justify each answer.
outline: Linearity follows from addition and scaling
Time invariance: delayed input delay gives delayed output
Causality: uses present and past input only
Stability: |y[n]|≤|x[n]|+|x[n−1]|≤2M for bounded input
Conclusion: linear, time-invariant, causal, BIBO stable

bank.q: Use the inner-product definition to test whether x₁(t)=1 and x₂(t)=cos(2πt) are orthogonal on 0≤t≤1. Then state the coefficient formula for expanding a signal in an orthogonal set {φₖ}.
outline: Inner product ⟨x₁,x₂⟩=∫₀¹ cos(2πt)dt
Integral equals zero, so the signals are orthogonal
Coefficient cₖ=⟨x,φₖ⟩/⟨φₖ,φₖ⟩
For orthonormal φₖ, cₖ=⟨x,φₖ⟩
State interval and conjugate for complex signals

bank.q: Compare energy signals and power signals. Show that a periodic signal with finite nonzero power is a power signal, and explain why a finite-energy signal has zero average power.
outline: Energy signal: finite E=∫|x(t)|²dt
Power signal: finite nonzero P=lim average of |x(t)|²
Periodic signal repeats; average power over one period is finite and nonzero
Total energy over infinite time for a nonzero periodic signal is infinite
For finite E, P=lim E/(2T)=0 as T→∞

bank.q: Analyse how the order of time shifting and time scaling affects the graph of x(3t−6). Give two correct sequences of operations and one wrong sequence, with sketches described.
outline: Write x(3t−6)=x(3(t−2))
Correct order 1: scale by 3 then shift right by 2
Correct order 2: shift right by 6 then scale by 3
Wrong order: shift right by 2 then scale by 3 gives x(3t−2)
Describe centre and width changes

bank.q: Evaluate the statement: 'A causal system is always stable, and a linear system is always time-invariant.' Give definitions and counterexamples or reasoning.
outline: Causality: output depends on present and past inputs only
Stability: every bounded input gives a bounded output
Counterexample causal but unstable: y(t)=eᵗx(t)
Linearity: superposition holds
Counterexample linear but time-varying: y(t)=t x(t)
Conclusion: the two statements are false; properties are independent

bank.q: An orthogonal set {φ₀,φ₁,...,φ_N} is used to represent a signal x(t) on an interval. Derive the coefficient formula, state Parseval's relation, and explain what completeness means for exact representation.
outline: Inner product ⟨x,φₖ⟩=∫x(t)φₖ*(t)dt
Coefficient cₖ=⟨x,φₖ⟩/⟨φₖ,φₖ⟩
For orthonormal set, cₖ=⟨x,φₖ⟩
Parseval: energy=Σ|cₖ|² when the basis is orthonormal
Completeness: no nonzero signal is orthogonal to every basis function, so error approaches zero

glossary.def: A function of an independent variable that carries information.
An operator that maps an input signal to an output signal.
The quantity on which a signal depends, usually time t or integer index n.
The value or strength of a signal at a chosen point or its peak scale.
A signal defined for every real value of time t.
A signal defined only at integer index n.
A value of a continuous-time signal taken at a fixed time instant.
A signal whose total energy E=∫|x(t)|²dt is finite.
A signal whose average power is finite and nonzero.
A signal that satisfies x(t+T)=x(t) for all t with some T>0.
The smallest positive T for which a periodic signal repeats.
A signal that satisfies x(−t)=x(t).
A signal that satisfies x(−t)=−x(t).
A generalized signal with zero width, unit area, and zero value except at the origin.
A signal that is zero before the origin and one after the origin.
A signal that is zero before the origin and rises linearly after it.
A signal of the form A·exp(st), where s may be real or complex.
A change x(t)→x(t−t₀) that moves a signal in time.
A change x(t)→x(at) that compresses or stretches a signal in time.
A change x(t)→x(−t) that flips a signal about the origin.
A system that obeys superposition for all inputs and constants.
A system whose response does not depend on the absolute time of the input.
A system whose output does not depend on future input values.
A system in which every bounded input produces a bounded output.
For signals, ⟨x,y⟩=∫x(t)y*(t)dt; it measures similarity and projection.
Signals whose inner product is zero on the chosen interval.
